title: Joining Ellington and the band's identifiable sound
summary: Bigard recalls arguing with Duke over his odd chords, the band working through the Depression, then a 1930 Cotton Club record is played.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, now, I know that, uh, today most people have an idea of what the Duke Ellington band sounds like. I mean, the minute you first hear the first few notes, you say, that's Duke Ellington. But I'm sure that when we start playing this next one, that, uh, if we weren't to identify the band, that might take them a bit of a time, unless there are real jazz buffs, to identify this sound. Because this one goes back to, I believe, about 1929, 1930, when Duke Ellington was at the Cotton Club. And we have one called, uh, Shout'em and Tilly. You remember this stage? Oh, yeah, I think so. All these things gotta come back to me. We'll go along after.

Because it's been so long. But there were good days, you know, and, uh, when I first joined Duke's band, and he used to arrange so weird, I used to think all these chords were wrong. Yeah. And he and I would have the biggest arguments and everything, but he'd prove it was right. And, uh, that's the way he's been. Of all the bands in the country, everybody could always identify Ellington when he came on the air. Right. And during the Depression, everybody wasn't working. Duke was working. Yeah. All through the Depression. We've never had a bit of trouble at all. Because people knew the band, I mean, and most of the things we played was his tune, though some of the tune of the guys in the band. Yeah. They were all originals. And so we went on.
